intro.title: ℹ️ About This Site
intro.description: "Dialect Pronunciation Atlas" (方音圖鑑) is an online platform for analyzing Middle Chinese categories, comparing dialects, and exploring geolinguistic patterns. It presents the historical layering of initials and finals, together with patterns of phonemic merger and split across dialect locations, in a clear and interactive form. The site brings together core phonological queries, dialect comparison, phonological analysis, historical character sets, interactive maps, character-list processing, public vocabulary and sentence data from the Chinese Language Resources Protection Project, village-data visualization, machine-learning analysis of natural-village names, Praat acoustic analysis, and dialect clustering. It is a comprehensive dialect-research platform that continues to grow.

feature1.heading: Core Queries
feature1.subtitle: Middle Chinese, Readings, Tones, Characters
feature1.intro: The site's earliest and central module, comprising four subpages.

items.title: Middle Chinese
items.body: Organize modern dialect readings by Middle Chinese categories. Users can freely combine rime group, rime, division, openness, tone, initial series, initial group, initial, voicing, place of articulation, and manner of articulation; the site automatically calculates the Cartesian product and removes invalid combinations. Location input supports fuzzy matching across simplified and traditional Chinese, as well as batch selection by region (Atlas Regions or MCPDict Regions). Results are displayed in tables, with multiple readings shown for polyphonic characters and distinct colors for literary and colloquial readings (red for literary, blue for colloquial, purple when the two share the same form, and green for ordinary polyphony). Statistics buttons open drill-down queries—for example, showing initial and tone distributions when examining finals. Clicking a phonetic value traces the source syllables, while clicking a place name opens detailed information about that dialect location. Multiple query windows can be compared in parallel, with phonetic-value filtering and Full or Primary display modes. The map view layers phonetic values by proportion, and map points also open drill-down queries. The phonological dataset can be switched; current options include Guangyun, the Dialect Survey Character List, Jiyun, Hongwu Zhengyun, and Old Chinese datasets.

items.title: Readings
items.body: Analyze the Middle Chinese sources of specific dialect readings. After entering syllables and locations, the results are presented in the same table and map formats. This query is computationally intensive, so using fewer locations is recommended.

items.title: Characters
items.body: Enter Chinese characters to view their readings and Middle Chinese categories across dialect locations. Results include annotations, while the map shows the geographical distribution of readings and supports literary/colloquial coloring.

items.title: Tones
items.body: View tone values and tone classes. The API is lightweight, and logged-in users can query multiple locations simultaneously without a fixed limit. Results are shown in tables, with tone classes distinguished by color. The map can display different tone classes, and clicking an item opens details about tone-class mergers.

feature2.heading: Interactive Maps & Custom Data
feature2.subtitle: Dialect Map, Regional Mapping, Custom Data, Map Drawing
feature2.intro: Corresponds to the 'Map' tab in the top navigation bar, containing four sub-pages.

items.title: Dialect Map
items.body: Switch query results to a map view with one click. Phonetic values are layered by proportion, and clicking a map point opens a drill-down query. Place-name labels, fullscreen mode, and basemap switching are supported.

items.title: Regional Mapping
items.body: Create dialect maps using Atlas Regions or MCPDict Regions, each with three selectable levels. Regions are shown in different colors; hovering or clicking reveals location names and regional information. The complete dataset can also be used to draw a nationwide regional map.

items.title: Custom Data
items.body: Users can import their own fieldwork data. The data are visible only to the owner, linked to the account, and synchronized across devices. Two organizational modes are supported: by survey location, for continually supplementing a single location; or by dialect feature, for continually adding locations to one feature and conducting geolinguistic comparisons.

items.title: Map Drawing
items.body: Provides online drawing tools with support for Voronoi diagrams and layer export.

feature3.heading: Dialect Comparison
feature3.subtitle: Compare Characters, Middle Chinese, Tone Classes, Phonetic Values
feature3.intro: Designed for quickly identifying similarities and differences among dialect locations, with four subpages.

items.title: Compare Characters
items.body: Select Chinese characters and dialect regions or locations. Green indicates identical readings, yellow partial agreement, and red complete difference, making cross-location similarities immediately visible. Fullscreen enlargement and pop-up views of detailed readings are supported. This can be used to examine the geographical distribution of particular phonological phenomena, such as lateral fricatives or palatalization.

items.title: Compare Middle Chinese
items.body: Define two sets of Middle Chinese criteria—for example, open Division I of the 宕 rime group versus open Division II of the 江 rime group—and compare complex phonological-category combinations across dialect locations. The similarity measure is defined as total overlap = Σ min(proportion in group 1, proportion in group 2). High overlap is shown in green, medium overlap in yellow, and low overlap in red. The method is simple and intuitive, works well for comparisons within the same location, and avoids problems caused by directly matching phoneme labels.

items.title: Compare Tone Classes
items.body: Analyze tone-class mergers across dialect locations, such as Yangshang merging with Yinqu or Yinru merging with Yangru. Multiple locations can be analyzed at once.

items.title: Compare Phonetic Values
items.body: Display the actual readings of multiple dialect locations side by side for direct, location-by-location comparison.

feature4.heading: In-Depth Analysis of Individual Dialects
feature4.subtitle: Phonological Systems, Phoneme Classification, Syllable Statistics, Sound Change
feature4.intro: Tools for detailed analysis of one or a small number of dialect locations, organized into four subpages.

items.title: Phonological Systems
items.body: Enter a dialect location to view its complete phonological matrix (initial × final × tone), with up to ten locations analyzed at once. Literary and colloquial readings are color-coded (red for literary, blue for colloquial, purple when the two share the same form, and green for ordinary polyphony). Cells are clickable for details, and fullscreen viewing is supported.

items.title: Phoneme Classification
items.body: Freely combine three dimensions—horizontal axis, vertical axis, and cell contents. For example, classify horizontally by voicing, vertically by place of articulation, and within cells by initial to count occurrences of each initial value. Alternatively, classify horizontally by openness, vertically by rime group, and within cells by division to organize final values. Clicking a cell opens its details.

items.title: Syllable Statistics
items.body: By default, data for all locations are shown through a pie chart of syllable proportions, a bar chart of the number of locations containing each syllable, and a scatter plot comparing syllable totals with the corresponding number of locations; larger circles represent more syllables. Every chart is clickable for detailed pop-ups. A custom-location mode supports up to 100 locations per analysis, counting initials, finals, and tones for each location, with a navigation wheel on the right for quick jumps.

items.title: Sound-Change Diagrams
items.body: Use Sankey diagrams, pie charts, and other visualizations to show how the initials, finals, and tones of a single dialect location developed from Middle Chinese to their modern forms, making merger and split pathways easy to see.

feature5.heading: Historical Character Sets
feature5.subtitle: Middle Chinese, Old Chinese, Early Modern Chinese, Cantonese Rime Books
feature5.intro: Browse the characters and Guangyun annotations under each phonological category by progressively expanding the hierarchy—the reverse direction of the Characters query, which starts from an entered character. The section covers four phonological systems across seven data tables.

items.title: Middle Chinese
items.body: The Guangyun system, organized hierarchically by rime group, openness, division, rime, tone, voicing, initial series, initial group, and initial. Guangyun annotations can be displayed, and the data can also be reorganized by initial labels, voicing, and other dimensions.

items.title: Old Chinese
items.body: Organized hierarchically by tone, initial, final, rime group, initial group, /r/ medial, and phonetic-series domain.

items.title: Early Modern Chinese
items.body: Includes three data tables: Zhongyuan Yinyun, Hongwu Zhengyun, and Menggu Ziyun.

items.title: Cantonese Rime Books
items.body: A hierarchical query based on the Fenyun Cuoyao system.

feature6.heading: Dialect Character-List Tools
feature6.subtitle: Character-List Validation, Jyutping to IPA, List Merging, List Derivation
feature6.intro: A practical toolkit for dialect fieldworkers, comprising four subpages.

items.title: Character-List Validation
items.body: Upload a dialect character list to automatically detect non-single-character entries, unusual phonetic symbols, missing tones, and other issues. The tool automatically separates initials, finals, and tones, and provides initial/final statistics together with tone-class and tone-value statistics. Online editing includes cell editing, batch editing of initials and finals, batch replacement of tone values, and row deletion; the revised file can then be downloaded. A command-line mode is retained for backward compatibility.

items.title: Jyutping to IPA
items.body: Upload a character list containing a "Jyutping" column and convert it to IPA according to configurable rules. Custom conversion rules are supported, and personal settings can be stored locally.

items.title: Merge Character Lists
items.body: Upload a reference list, which determines the final order, together with the lists to merge. Column names are detected automatically (character columns: 單字/phrase/汉字/漢字; transcription columns: IPA/ipa/音標/音标/syllable). Annotations are stored as Excel comments, multiple readings are separated with semicolons, and missing characters are appended at the end.

items.title: Character-List Derivation
items.body: Automatically infer and generate missing readings according to phonological rules.

feature7.heading: Vocabulary and Sentence Data
feature7.subtitle: Language Preservation Vocabulary, Grammar (50 Sentences), Yangchun Colloquial Vocabulary
feature7.intro: Based on public data from the Chinese Language Resources Protection Project. The site currently includes 1,000 vocabulary items from 1,247 dialect locations, together with the project's 50-sentence grammar dataset. All data come from the project's official public platform.

items.title: Language Preservation Vocabulary
items.body: Available in map, card, and table views. When the map is zoomed out, dialect locations are clustered; zooming in reveals individual vocabulary entries. The display can switch among glosses, IPA transcriptions, and place names, and every point opens a detailed pop-up. Card view presents place name, vocabulary, annotation, pronunciation, and region information, with search matching. Table view supports search, sorting on every column, and pop-up filters with multi-select and inverse selection.

items.title: Language Preservation Grammar (50 Sentences)
items.body: Also available in card, table, and map views. Entries can be searched by place name, written form, or syllable and filtered by dialect region.

items.title: Yangchun Colloquial Vocabulary
items.body: A collection of commonly used colloquial vocabulary from the Yangchun area.

feature8.heading: Natural Village Data
feature8.subtitle: Guangdong Hierarchy, Interactive Map, Raw Data, Yangchun Natural Villages, Machine Learning
feature8.intro: Provides geographical, administrative, and dialect information for natural villages. The site includes a Guangdong natural-village hierarchy, an interactive map, raw data tables, a dedicated Yangchun dataset, and machine-learning analyses.

items.title: Guangdong Natural-Village Hierarchy
items.body: Based on dialect data for Guangdong natural villages entered from the Quan Yue Cunqing series. The author recorded the villages manually, one by one, with most current data concentrated in western Guangdong, including Yangjiang, Maoming, and Yunfu. The hierarchy can be expanded from city → county or district → town → administrative village → natural village, clearly showing administrative relationships and supporting search.

items.title: Interactive Map
items.body: Natural-village points are clustered when the map is zoomed out; zooming in reveals individual village names and dialect data. The data can be filtered by city, county, and town, and the map remains responsive during free zooming. Users can switch between village-name and dialect-data displays.

items.title: Raw Data Table
items.body: Displays the original Guangdong natural-village data with filtering and search matching.

items.title: Yangchun Natural Villages
items.body: A specially compiled and proofread dataset based on the Yangchun County Gazetteer. It uses etymologically appropriate characters rather than homophonous substitutes, making it more accurate and faster to load than the general Quan Yue Cunqing dataset.

items.title: Machine Learning Analysis (VillagesML)
items.body: A complete standalone sub-application containing seven modules and 28 analysis tabs: Character Analysis (frequency tendencies, embedding similarity, character networks, significance); Semantic Analysis (category labels, combination patterns, N-gram analysis, semantic indices, semantic networks, subcategory analysis); Spatial Analysis (spatial hotspots, spatial clustering, spatial visualization, spatial integration); Pattern Analysis (frequency analysis, structural analysis, tendency analysis, N-gram exploration, N-gram statistics); Regional Analysis (aggregate statistics, feature vectors, category tendencies, similarity analysis); ML Computation (basic clustering, character tendencies, sampled villages, spatially aware clustering, hierarchical clustering, feature extraction, subset analysis); and Search.

feature9.heading: Web-Based Praat Acoustic Analysis
feature9.subtitle: Pitch, Formants, Vowel Space, F0-Based Tone Estimation
feature9.intro: Praat's core algorithms are integrated into the backend through praat-parselmouth, so acoustic analysis can be performed directly in the browser without installing additional software. Login is required because the algorithms are CPU-intensive and server resources are limited.

items.title: Audio Upload and Trimming
items.body: Supports drag-and-drop uploads in WAV, MP3, M4A, WebM, OGG, FLAC, AAC, and other formats, as well as direct recording on the site. After recording, users can drag to select and trim segments without separate editing software. Mobile devices are supported; phone recording is recommended because it often provides better audio quality than a computer microphone.

items.title: Two Analysis Modes
items.body: Single-syllable mode precisely isolates one syllable and is best suited to vowel-space analysis. Continuous-speech mode performs automatic segmentation on the backend and may introduce some error, but it is useful for F0-based tone estimation: multiple tone classes can be uploaded together to generate a five-level tone chart using Shi Feng's T-value method.

items.title: Seven Analysis Modules
items.body: Basic information (audio duration and sampling rate); F0 analysis (tone-value features, five-level tone calculation, F0 curve); intensity analysis (mean intensity, intensity range, intensity trajectory); formant analysis (formant trajectories); voice-quality analysis (harmonics-to-noise ratio, jitter, shimmer); segment analysis (single syllable → rime_core + syllable_like; continuous speech → voiced / speech / silence); spectrogram analysis (frequency–time energy distribution, limited to audio no longer than three seconds).

items.title: Precision
items.body: Three modes are available: Fast, Standard, and High Precision.

items.title: Vowel Space
items.body: Displays vowel values and their movement trajectories. For best results, use single-syllable mode in a quiet environment and trim the segment precisely. For example, the vowel in the Yangchun Cantonese reading of 「你」 can be seen moving from ɛ down toward æ and then upward toward ɨ.

items.title: F0-Based Tone Estimation
items.body: Extract the voiced or rime_core portion of each tone class, add the segments to a list, and generate a five-level tone chart using Shi Feng's T-value method. Results can be exported to Excel. Multiple tone classes may be extracted from a single recording, and the workflow is also convenient on mobile devices.

feature10.heading: Dialect Clustering
feature10.subtitle: Multi-Location Clustering and Visualization
feature10.intro: Provides a multi-panel workspace for entering dialect locations, managing clustering tasks, and viewing workflows and results. It can be used to explore relationships and grouping patterns among dialect locations and to provide quantitative evidence for dialect classification.

intro.footer: Welcome to "Dialect Pronunciation Atlas"—explore the historical layers of dialects with us!

reflection.title: 🧑‍💻 Reflections
reflection.paragraph1: It began simply as a convenience for my own research: I wrote a few Python scripts to process dialect data. Later, I organized them into a FastAPI backend and built a modest single-page interface with vanilla JavaScript. My ambition at the time was uncomplicated—a tool that felt comfortable to use would have been enough. I never expected the project to keep growing until, almost without notice, a year had passed. That year brought disappointment in the postgraduate entrance examination, anxiety about employment, and the farewells of graduation. My state of mind shifted again and again, yet in the quiet of writing code I always found a small corner in which to settle myself.
reflection.paragraph2: Over that year, I gradually became acquainted with front-end development. At the beginning of 2026, I spent three months interning as a front-end developer at an internet company, and during that period I carefully rewrote the entire project in Vue. Over the following months, I added dialect comparison, character-list processing, vocabulary and sentence data from the Chinese Language Resources Protection Project, village-data visualization, Praat acoustic analysis, and more. Writing code was also a way of studying phonology: building a sound query workflow often required first clarifying the phonological information behind it, while a deeper understanding of phonology continually inspired new features. Technology and scholarship nourished one another, allowing the project to become steadily more complete.
reflection.paragraph3: Today, the site receives roughly 300 visits and 5,000 API calls each day. The journey from command-line scripts to an online platform has not been straightforward, but seeing people genuinely use it—and knowing that it has helped many language enthusiasts and even university researchers—makes every effort feel worthwhile. My sincere thanks go to everyone who has offered support, encouragement, or a response. If the site can save you even a little time spent searching through reference materials, it has fulfilled its purpose.
reflection.poem:
May the voices of every region live on;
May the beauty of Chinese characters always be cherished;
May the flame of civilization endure through every interaction and every moment of resonance.

zhongguInputMode.description: Choose between the dropdown selector or direct-input modes for Middle Chinese queries. Direct input supports Middle Chinese category expressions such as "泥母 庄组 蟹-等", as well as direct character queries.
